newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Eurobond bubble bigger after record year.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Eurobond bubble bigger after record year.

text.p: After a year of record issuance and tighter spreads in all sectors in the Eurobond market, some syndicate managers think 1997 could see the balloon deflate.

"The market is at high levels in terms of price, and spreads are at record tight levels, so the possibility for a correction at some point next year is undoubtedly there," J.P. Morgan's Eurobond syndicate head Paul Hearn said.
WestMerchant head of syndicate Martin Hatt agreed.
Volume of issuance has hit a record $650 billion thus far in 1996, versus around $460 billion last year.
The new issues market has grown at an average rate of 20 percent per annum since 1980 as new products and structures are added and new currencies are tapped.
But despite the possibility of a correction in prices in the secondary market and a cooling off of Eurobond supply if key interest rates rise, syndicate managers prefer to remain bullish.
"They (syndicate officials) will go into anything that will generate volume and profit so if one area goes quiet, they'll explore another", a dealer said.
"It does not matter, business will go on."
The feel-good factor is based on expectations of benign government bond markets, an environment conducive to the issuance of high-yielding paper.
Morgan Stanley's syndicate manager Eden Riche said: "The themes and trends this year are likely to continue should there be no shocks."
"Activity should be at or exceed this year's because all the markets have done very well and we have seen new growth areas like the asset-backed sector," Riche said.
Primary market participants said grounds for optimism included increased liquidity and record redemptions due next year.
The first six months of next year will see around $62 billion worth of dollar redemptions alone, according to Capital DATA Bondware.
Syndicate manager David Tory of top bookrunner for 1996 Merrill Lynch said the U.S. house remained firmly bullish for 1997. "You've got to be optimistic," he said.
THE BUBBLE WILL NOT BURST

"The reasons the bubble will not burst is that next year we are going to see tremendous amounts of liquidity and record redemptions which will pump a lot of money back into the market and on that basis I think we have a relatively similar year to this year," Tory said.
He said there was going to be a lot of cash coming back into the system and with U.S. equity markets at a peak, there could be a flow of funds into the capital markets.
"I don't think spreads will tighten much further in the triple-A or double-A sectors but there will be other products in the market to fill in the gaps," Tory said.

Market expectations are that the dollar will remain the darling of the primary market but that in the run-up to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) the mark will find favour as a good Euro-hedge.
"Most of the issuance will be in dollars early next year with marks featuring later in the year," UBS director of mark new issues in Frankfurt Jan Marc Fergg said.
In the never-ceasing investor quest for high-yielding paper more supply of new products such as asset-backed paper is expected.
Emerging market paper from Latin America and Eastern Europe is expected to flourish, with subordinated debt seen as a growth area.
